newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Kepco sterling debut, EBRD too.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Kepco sterling debut, EBRD too.

text.p: Korea Electric Power came to the market with its debut sterling bond on Tuesday, while more details emerged on the EBRD's won bond launched on Monday.
Kepco launched a 150 million sterling bond due April 2007 via lead manager SBC Warburg.
The bond will be priced to yield 78 basis points over 10-year Sterling government bonds. Fees are 35 basis points.
The bond is the second-ever sterling-denominated debt issue launched by a South Korean entity and the first fixed-rate bond.
Last week, Korea Development Bank launched a 150 million sterling three-year floating rate note issue that pays a coupon of 12.5 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate.

While KDB's three-year FRN appealed to bank investors throughout Europe, the Kepco fixed-rate bond was snapped up by U.K. institutional investors and fund managers, said Chris van Niekerk, executive director of debt capital markets at SBC Warburg.

Van Niekerk said he was "fantastically encouraged" by investors response to the issue. He noted that UK fund managers are familiar with utility credits because they are active investors in domestic utility bonds.
He said investors taking the Kepco paper were unperturbed by troubles in Korea's financial sector because Kepco was viewed as isolated from the type of bad loan problems facing the banks.
Lead manager KDB Securities released further details on the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's won-denominated bond, which was launched on Monday.
Both the domestic and international tranches of the 94.8 billion won bond have final maturities of five years and pay semi-annual coupons of 10 percent.
The 71.1 billion domestic tranche was priced at 92.57 to yield 12.02 percent, or 63 basis points below three-year bank guaranteed Korean corporate bonds.
The 23.7 billion won international tranche was priced at 100.25 percent to yield 9.935 percent on a semi-annual basis.
Merrill Lynch International is lead manager along with KDB Securities for the international tranche.

Colin Blackwell, head of syndications at Merrill Lynch, on Tuesday took issue with the notion that the World Bank, rather than the EBRD, was the first out of the block with a won issue sold to international investors.
The World Bank launched its won bond last Friday, but Blackwell said the issue has not yet closed and that participants still are awaiting their allocations.
The EBRD issue has been freed to trade.
The EBRD's foreign tranche pays an annual yield of 10.182 percent.

Blackwell said that because there is no benchmark for offshore won bonds and because the won is not fully convertible, the deal's yield was determined by assessing the won's value in the non-deliverable forward market.

"We calculated that rate to be about 10 to 11.20 percent, and because this is a pure vanilla instrument and the EBRD is a AAA credit, we think it rational that the yield should be at the tighter end of the market," he said.

Yen-denominated funds were expected to be big investors in the bond because at over 10 percent, the yield pick-up over low-yielding yen assets is considered large enough to offset any unfavourable currency movements.
In loans, Hong Kong's Sun Hung Kai Properties said it would soon launch its HK$10.5 billion revolving credit/term loan facility.
